r1.h: Before you start: your full checklist
p: Syllabus section 5, 'What else you need to know', starts with 'Before you start'. Use this checklist.
• Previous study: no previous study of Religious Studies is expected. Start with the basics and check students' English reading level.
• Guided learning hours: about 130 for the subject. Add up your real lessons. This is guidance only. Needs vary with the school and the learners' experience.
• Availability: this syllabus is not available in all administrative zones. Check www.cambridgeinternational.org/0490.
• Timetable: find your zone's timetable at www.cambridgeinternational.org/timetables. Give the dates to your exams officer.
• Exam series: you can enter candidates in the November series.
• Syllabus year: use the syllabus for the year the candidate takes the exam. This course follows the 2025, 2026 and 2027 syllabus.
• Private candidates: they can enter. Read the Cambridge Guide to Making Entries.
• Combining syllabuses: the only exceptions are Cambridge O Level Biblical Studies 2035 and syllabuses with the same title at the same level.
• Group awards: Cambridge ICE recognises success in a range of subjects.

b: Write down your guided learning hours.
Confirm availability and zone timetable.
Check the syllabus year.
Share the dates with your exams officer.
Note any students who may need access arrangements.

r1.h: Making entries: step-by-step with the exams officer
p: Syllabus section 5 also explains 'Making entries'. Teachers and exams officers work together.
• Who: exams officers submit entries to Cambridge International.
• What they need from you: the number of candidates, whether any are private candidates, whether anyone needs access arrangements, and the right components (Paper 1 and Paper 2 for all candidates).
• Entry option codes and instructions: in the Cambridge Guide to Making Entries. Your exams officer has a copy.

• Exam administration: to keep exams secure, papers are produced for different administrative zones. Each zone has its own timetable. An entry option code identifies the components a candidate takes for that zone.
• Support: Cambridge supports exams officers at www.cambridgeinternational.org/eoguide.
• Retakes: candidates can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want. See www.cambridgeinternational.org/retakes.
• Language: the syllabus and assessment materials are in English only.

ex.t: A simple entry timeline (adapt to your exam series)
b: Start of the course: check availability, zone and access arrangements.
Several months before the exam: confirm candidate numbers and final entries with the exams officer.
Before the exam: confirm the timetable, rooms and invigilation.
After the exam: wait for results and plan any retakes.

r2.h: Accessibility and equality: the full picture for teachers
p: Syllabus section 5 has a heading 'Accessibility and equality' with two parts.

• Syllabus and assessment design: Cambridge works to avoid direct or indirect discrimination. It designs syllabuses and assessment materials to be as inclusive as possible for candidates of all national, cultural or social backgrounds and candidates with protected characteristics (special educational needs and disability, religion and belief, characteristics related to gender and identity). Language and layout are designed to make the materials accessible, so that all candidates have the fairest chance to show their knowledge, skills and understanding. This reduces the need for reasonable adjustments.

• Access arrangements: including modified papers. They are the main way Cambridge meets its duty, as guided by the UK Equality Act (2010), to make reasonable adjustments for candidates with SEN, disability, illness or injury. They help when a candidate would otherwise be at a substantial disadvantage.
How this helps you teach Religious Studies:
• Notice early which students need support with reading, writing, hearing or sight.
• Use clear, short sentences and glossaries of religious terms.
• Never ask students to reveal their own faith to take part.

ex.t: Examples of barriers and arrangements (to discuss with your exams officer)
b: A student with dyslexia may need extra time or a modified paper.
A student with a hearing difficulty may need adjustments to oral instructions.
A student with an injury to their writing hand may need support to write.
Check the Cambridge Handbook for what is allowed.

r2.h: After the exam: reading results and certificates
p: Syllabus section 5 explains 'After the exam'.
• Grades A*, A, B, C, D, E, F or G show the standard achieved. A* is the highest, G is the lowest.
• Ungraded: the performance did not meet the standard required for grade G. It is reported on the statement of results but not on the certificate.
• Q (pending) and X (no result): may appear on statements of results, not on the certificate.
• On results and certificates the qualification is shown as International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE).
• For 0490, candidates sit two papers (80 marks each) and receive one overall grade from A* to G.
After results, what should teachers do?
• Check every student's result against expectations.
• Ask your exams officer about retakes, and about Cambridge results services.
• Use results to plan teaching for the next year.

b: Start with what they did well.
Explain the grade in plain words.
Show the next step: retake, AS or A Level, or another course.
Keep the tone kind and honest.

r2.h: How students and teachers can use the grades: worked examples
p: The syllabus names two purposes of assessment: to measure learning and achievement, and to show likely future success.
Use for students:
• A student with grade B or above in 0490 may be well prepared for AS Level Divinity or Islamic Studies and for subjects that need essay writing and evaluation.
• A student with grade D may need to strengthen evaluation skills before AS Level, or may choose another route.
• Grades help students choose courses and careers.
Use for teachers:
• Compare your class results with last year's results.
• Look for the questions and topics where marks were lost, using results analysis and principal examiner reports.
• Compare AO1 and AO2: if students did well on knowledge but poorly on evaluation, teach more part (c) practice.
• Set targets and write actions: for example, 'Add one evaluation task to every unit'.
• Share results with colleagues to improve the whole department.

b: Class average: AO1 strong, AO2 weak.
Action: weekly 15-minute evaluation practice with the PEEL-J pattern.
Check progress after four weeks with a short test.
Share improvements at the next staff meeting.

r2.h: Grade descriptions: how to prepare while they are unpublished
p: The syllabus has a heading 'Grade descriptions'. Grade descriptions give an idea of the standards of achievement that candidates awarded certain grades are likely to show. A weakness in one part of the exam can be balanced by better performance in another.
The syllabus says grade descriptions for Religious Studies will be published after the first assessment in 2025. What to do now:
• Check the Cambridge website and the School Support Hub for updates and sign up for syllabus update emails.
• Use the specimen mark schemes and levels-of-response grids to understand standards.
• Use examiner reports as they become available.
• Keep a folder of sample answers at different levels, with notes on why they earned those marks.

ex.t: Build your own working scale (a classroom tool, not an official grade description)
b: Strong: accurate detail, clear explanation, several views with evidence, reasoned judgement.
Secure: mostly accurate, some explanation, two views, simple judgement.
Developing: some facts, little explanation, one view, no clear judgement.
Replace with official descriptions when published.

r2.h: Changes to this syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027: what to do about each
p: The syllabus was reviewed and revised for first examination in 2025. Cambridge says you must read the whole syllabus before planning your teaching.
Make a list of what to do with each change.
• More detailed subject content: use the lettered points in Section 3 as your checklist, but do not teach more than the syllabus asks.
• Some content added or removed: compare any old notes with the new Section 3.
• New topic, Stewardship of the environment (all three religions): add a lesson in the Religion and social action block. Animal ethics is not included.
• New topic, five roots of Usul ad-Din (Islam): add a lesson on Shi'ah beliefs.
• Removed Christianity content: difference between a bishop and an archbishop; types of Bible literature (history, myth, psalms, songs, prophecy); tithing.
• Removed Islam content: Jihad (greater and lesser).
• Removed Judaism content: knowledge of the Tenakh, Mishnah and Talmud; the festivals Simchat Torah and Shavuot.
• Content divided between Paper 1 and Paper 2.
• In Judaism, G-d is spelt G-d.
• Some section names changed slightly.
• Learner attributes were added to the syllabus.

b: Take your old scheme of work and cross out removed topics.
Highlight new topics in a different colour.
Check textbooks and websites for removed content.
Note any new resources you need.
